summary:
We developed an interactive 3D navigation application, essentially "Google Maps for Mars," that guides astronauts across the Martian surface without relying on GPS. Using a third-person interface, the app displays the astronaut's rover, suit, planned route, landmarks, and surrounding terrain in real time.

To address the challenge of traversing an uncharted, GPS-free environment, the app combines onboard sensors with 3D terrain-mapping technology inspired by NASA rovers. It automatically detects local hazards, including cliffs, craters, boulders, steep slopes, soft sand, and radiation zones. Once a threat is identified, the app warns the astronaut of the specific danger and dynamically calculates a safer detour.

This tool is critical for astronaut safety and mission success. Because significant communication delays between Earth and Mars prevent mission control from providing immediate, real-time directions, astronauts need reliable autonomous navigation to ensure they never lose their way or wander into life-threatening terrain.

details:
ARES NAV is a GPS-free 3D surface navigation system built for astronauts and rovers exploring Mars's Jezero Crater. Using third-person chase, orbital, or top-down views, it renders a 5.12 km by 5.12 km terrain model with six data layers: Optical, Slope, Regolith, Boulders, Radiation, and Composite Risk. A terrain solver detects five hazard classes (steep slopes, boulder fields, soft regolith, radiation zones, and craters) and uses weighted A* pathfinding to plot safe routes and suggest detours. By bridging orbital reconnaissance with real-time ground decisions, the project aims to prevent route hazards, extend safe EVA ranges, and streamline geological sample logging.

  • Offline Autonomy: Running all routing, hazard sweeps, and AI safety checks locally overcomes the 12-minute, 41-second Earth-Mars communication delay and dust-storm blackouts.
  • Unified Survival Telemetry: Consolidating navigation, suit oxygen reserves, weather forecasts, crew locations, and an SOS rescue beacon into one screen reduces cognitive load during extravehicular activities.
  • Realistic Mission Physics: The team modeled distinct rover (2.8 m/s) versus EVA suit (1.15 m/s) travel speeds alongside strict life-support limits, including a 20% oxygen reserve floor and a 25 mSv radiation soft limit.
  • Field Usability: Floating 3D labels use screen-space collision detection and UI occlusion checks so landmarks never cover controls.

The website was developed using Arena AI. Under the hood, it is built with HTML5, CSS3, vanilla JavaScript, and GLSL shaders, utilizing native WebGL for 3D rendering and HTML5 2D Canvas for charts and the minimap. Its custom procedural engine is informed by NASA Trek, USGS Astrogeology, NASA Worldview, and Mars 2020 datasets, and runs smoothly on GPU-accelerated displays via adaptive resolution scaling. What makes the project creative is its zero-dependency 3D engine coded inside a single self-contained file, paired with dynamic environmental events where dust storms simultaneously darken the sky, cut solar power, and trigger offline autonomy mode.
